Un père Noël pour célébrer la diversité: A Santa Claus to Celebrate Diversity
Et si le père Noël était noir ? Asiatiqu: What if Santa Claus were Black? Asian? Arab? Latino?

Et si le père Noël était noir ? Asiatiqu: What if Santa Claus were Black? Asian? Arab? Latino? When we think of the famous resident of the North Pole, the image that immediately comes to mind is a portly white man dressed in red, with a beard as white as he is. Yet the children he brings presents to by the thousands every year are far from all Caucasian. In Montréal, a few rare initiatives are trying to bring more diversity into the magic of Christmas.
« Ho ho ho ! » Dès l’entrée du père Noël: “Ho ho ho!” As soon as Santa walked into the party organized by event company Mkali Moments on December 16, the children’s cries of joy rang through the room. It’s a scene that repeats itself in every Christmas market and shopping centre during the holiday season. But one difference stands out: this Santa is Black. It’s a rare choice, and one the event’s organizer proudly stands by.
<strong>‍</strong>\n« Quand j’ai créé mo: ‍ “When I started my business three years ago, I wanted to organize a Christmas party for kids. I had never seen a Black Santa growing up, so I thought it would be nice. As an adult, I realized I had never seen a Santa who looks like me,” recalls Jacqueline Dzandu, a Quebecer of Ghanaian origin. Beyond skin colour, she wants to offer children another representation of this character they love so much.
« Au début, je pensais avoir un public p: “At first, I thought my audience would be mostly from the community, but you can see that families from all backgrounds are coming to share this friendly moment,” she says happily. More than 150 people did indeed come to enjoy the children’s activities (face painting, games, a visit from the Snow Queen…) as well as the market of local entrepreneurs.
Rien, dans l’invitation diffusée par Mka: Nothing in the invitation circulated by Mkali Moments indicated that Santa would be different, other than a discreet emoji with ebony skin. Some parents, surprised at first, were quick to praise the initiative.
<strong>‍</strong>\n« L’innocence est la: ‍ “Innocence is a child’s best defence,” wrote Lao She in Un fils tombé du ciel, in 1934. Between innocence and the dazzling aura of this mythical white-bearded figure, no child seems bothered by the skin colour of their idol. “It’s really cool, I had never seen that, and my daughter didn’t say a single thing,” says Misha, an Australian musician and vendor at the event. “I think she doesn’t see the difference in colour, and I’m very happy about that.”
Un constat largement partagé. « Je n’ava: It’s a widely shared observation. “I had never seen this before. I think the idea that Santa is white has been perpetuated for decades without anyone even questioning it, when we’re not all white. My kids are happy, all they see is Santa! And it’s funny, because if you look closely at the pattern on my kids’ outfits, they’re Black Santa heads,” says Tracey, an Indigenous woman from Montréal. On Santa’s knees, her boys, aged three years and six months, smile for the photo.
« J’ai été surprise, mais vraiment conte: “I was surprised, but really glad! The children didn’t see any difference, and I loved their reaction. People need to be aware that humans are all the same, and that starts at a very young age,” says Sherley, founder of Shey Accessoires, who is showcasing her jewellery.
Les uns après les autres, les bambins én: One after another, the little ones list for Santa the gifts they hope to find under the tree on the morning of December 25. Some are so moved that they jump around and can barely contain their excitement. All it takes is asking them what they think of this Santa to understand that ethnicity doesn’t even cross their minds: “He’s so handsome!”
Pourtant, le pari était loin d’être gagn: Still, the bet was far from a sure thing for Mkali Moments. Starting with the difficult search for a Black Santa.
<strong>‍</strong>\nLa diversité est à c: ‍ Diversity is so rare in the brotherhood of Santas that simply looking for a Black one is like searching for a needle in a haystack. The Agence des Pères Noël professionnels du Québec, located in Repentigny, doesn’t offer this kind of profile. “That’s not a request that comes from the shopping centres we serve,” it explains pragmatically. No demand, so no supply. But doesn’t supply often create demand? Every year, Mkali Moments has to deal with this reality.
« Quand j’ai commencé, il y a trois ans,: “When I started three years ago, I didn’t really know where to find a Black Santa,” says the event’s organizer with a laugh. “I talked to people around me, and an acquaintance gave me someone’s name. The second year, that person wasn’t available, so I bought a nice costume and someone close to me took care of it. This year, I had found someone, but when I got back in touch with him a few weeks ago, I got no answer.” Once again, Jacqueline Dzandu had to turn to her loved ones for help. In the end, it was her father-in-law who agreed to put on the red suit.
<em>La fondatrice de Mkali Moments, Jacq: Mkali Moments founder Jacqueline Dzandu, alongside her father-in-law, Soney, a.k.a. Santa Claus. (Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy)
« J’adore le concept du père Noël noir,: “I love the concept of a Black Santa, so I didn’t hesitate to do it for her. Everything to do with Christmas can’t be white!” exclaims the man who goes by Soney in everyday life. He is 57 and arrived from Ghana four years ago. He works in maintenance at a CIUSSS while waiting for his optician’s diploma to be recognized, a difficult process.
En attendant, Soney se réjouit d’offrir: In the meantime, Soney is delighted to offer children a colourful representation of Santa. “It’s the first time I’ve done it; I didn’t know what to expect, but the children are so happy that I could do it again every year. There was a little boy who was so excited to see Santa that he walked past everyone to give me a hug – I think that’s incredible. Things don’t happen by magic, you have to make them happen,” he says.
S’il est difficile de battre en brèche l: While it’s hard to break down the cliché that Santa is a white man, delving into the historical origins of this iconic figure helps dispel such prejudices. What if Santa really were Black?
<strong>‍</strong>\nÀ l’origine, Noël es: ‍ Christmas was originally a pagan festival of the Roman Empire marking the winter solstice, on December 21. It celebrated the return of light as the days grew longer and nature was reborn. “Once Christianity became the state religion in 313 under Emperor Constantine, the Church looked for a date to symbolize the birth of Jesus, whose actual date is unknown. It chose this period, when light was already being celebrated, to symbolize the light of the world and the first great mystery of Jesus’s birth,” explains Catherine Foisy, a professor of socio-religious history at Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM).
Quant au mythe du père Noël, son apparit: As for the myth of Santa Claus, its much later appearance is tied to a historical figure. “The character of Santa Claus was built from the more or less mythical story of Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra in the 4th<sup></sup> century AD. The story goes that he resurrected children who had been cut up by a butcher and that he gave gifts to children every year. He certainly wasn’t white, since he came from the region of Lycia, in present-day Turkey. He must have had a much darker complexion than the way he is depicted today. It’s worth noting that all figures in religious iconography are shown as white, starting with Christ himself, whose Western depiction doesn’t match what scientific advances have allowed us to discover,” says the historian. It’s a form of cultural appropriation that persists today.
Plus tard, la tradition de saint Nicolas: Later, the tradition of Saint Nicholas took root in Europe before crossing the ocean. “He was widely celebrated in the Netherlands. Dutch immigrants were the ones who introduced, on this side of the Atlantic, the figure they called Sinterklaas – who would become Santa Claus in the United States in the 18th century. Then it was the cartoonist Thomas Nast who, in 1845, gave Santa his features for the first time, with his beard, his home at the North Pole, his lists of well-behaved children…” says Pierre Lahoud, co-author of Noël et ses traditions au Québec.
Finalement, le capitalisme a repris cett: Finally, capitalism took this image over for marketing purposes, creating the commercial holiday we know today. “People often talk about Coca-Cola, but they didn’t create Santa Claus, they publicized him. The idea of a white Santa was perpetuated because the Western Church was white at the time and wanted symbols that would speak to the people, even though there’s a good chance Saint Nicholas had a darker complexion. But I think this holiday is becoming pagan again and that, within a few years, we’ll have much greater diversity in Christmas iconography,” he says. It’s a prediction that remains to be confirmed.
L’ancêtre du père Noël n’avait pas la co: Santa’s ancestor was not the colour of eternal snow. In fact, Santa takes on the features of those who celebrate him. In India, for example, Christmas Baba has brown skin. “I was born here, this is my culture. But Montréal is a multicultural city, so I simply think it’s good that this diversity is also visible at Christmas,” says Jacqueline Dzandu.
